faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars that orbit their common center of mass, aligned so that their orbital plane points toward Earth. As they orbit, one star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. From our perspective, the total brightness of the system dips in a regular pattern. This produces a distinctive signature in a light curve - a plot of brightness over time.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is any star that passes our statistical vetting and appears novel when cross-checked against known catalogs. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that has also passed the automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the eclipse signal actually comes from the target star and is not caused by a nearby star. Confirmation here means it passed our pipeline - not that it has been independently verified by other astronomers or added to scientific databases.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and 'confirmed' on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model trained on 2,448 labeled examples, which compares favorably to our rule-based baseline pipeline. It serves as a second opinion on candidate quality. However, it is not currently used to gate, filter, or prioritize which candidates receive the pixel-level check - every candidate that passes statistical vetting and the novelty cross-match receives one. The ML score is available for research purposes only.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?

faqs.answer: Each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check that examines the spatial distribution of the eclipse signal within the target's pixel stamp from TESS data. This check confirms that the brightness variations come from the target star itself rather than from a nearby star whose signal bled into the target's photometry. The entire check is performed automatically by our pipeline.
faqs.question: How are candidates checked for real signals?

faqs.answer: Sometimes a light curve can look periodic at exactly half its true orbital period if the eclipses have unequal depths - you might see every eclipse, but measure the period incorrectly. Our pipeline tests for this by comparing the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If they differ significantly, we flag this as a potential period alias, though some candidates may carry this caveat and still be listed.
faqs.question: What is the period-alias check?

faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate on this site links to its light curve and detailed measurements. You can download TESS data yourself, inspect the eclipses, and check our reported orbital periods and eclipse depths. We encourage independent scrutiny. Keep in mind that confirmation here means it passed our pixel-level check - not that all possible caveats have been ruled out.

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of our pipeline's work. We do not perform follow-up observations, submit candidates to astronomical databases, or track their status after they appear here. Individual candidates may inspire follow-up by other researchers, but that is beyond the scope of this project. Each candidate's page may note open questions or caveats that warrant further study.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary star systems in data from NASA's TESS satellite. When two stars orbit each other and their orbital plane aligns with Earth, one star periodically blocks light from the other, creating a characteristic dip in brightness. Our pipeline samples target stars from TESS, measures the light curves, applies statistical tests to separate real eclipsing binaries from noise and instrumental artifacts, cross-checks against six major variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and then performs an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby star. So far we have confirmed 238 candidates from a sample of 16,573 targets - representing 1.9% of TESS's full target list. Candidates carry caveats; some pages note open questions. Each result on this site has passed our automated vetting pipeline, but individual candidates may warrant additional scrutiny or follow-up by other researchers.
